module: C6 Rate and Extent of Reactions

Rate of Reaction.intro: The rate of a reaction measures how quickly reactants are converted to products. It can be measured by how quickly a reactant is used up or a product is formed.

sections.title: Measuring Rate
points: Rate = amount of product formed (or reactant used) ÷ time
Methods: measure gas volume produced, mass lost, colour change intensity, precipitate formation
Rate is highest at the start — most reactant present
Rate decreases over time as reactants are used up
Reaction is complete when graph becomes flat

callout.label: Calculating Rate
callout.text: Draw a tangent to the curve at the point of interest. Rate = gradient = rise ÷ run. For mean rate: total change ÷ total time.

keyTerms.def: The speed at which reactants are converted to products
Total amount of change divided by total time taken
A straight line that touches a curve at one point — used to find the rate at that instant

examTips: Steeper gradient on a graph = faster rate.
Flat line on a graph = reaction complete (not necessarily slow).
Initial rate (start of graph) is always the fastest.
commonMistakes: Confusing a flat line (reaction complete) with a slow rate.
Calculating mean rate instead of instantaneous rate when asked for rate at a specific point.

Factors Affecting Rate.intro: Several factors affect how quickly a reaction occurs. All explanations should be linked to collision theory.

sections.title: Collision Theory
sections.text: For a reaction to occur, particles must collide with energy greater than or equal to the activation energy. More frequent, higher-energy collisions = faster rate.

sections.title: The Five Factors
points: Temperature — higher temp gives particles more kinetic energy; collide more frequently AND with more energy; rate increases significantly
Concentration (solutions) — more particles in same volume; more frequent collisions
Pressure (gases) — same as concentration — particles closer together, more frequent collisions
Surface area — smaller pieces expose more surface; more particles available to collide
Catalyst — provides alternative reaction pathway with lower activation energy; not used up

callout.label: Catalysts
callout.text: A catalyst lowers the activation energy — shown on an energy profile as a lower peak. It does NOT change the overall energy change (ΔH) or the equilibrium position.

keyTerms.def: Reactions occur when particles collide with sufficient energy (≥ activation energy)
Minimum energy needed for a successful collision
Substance that speeds up a reaction by providing a lower activation energy pathway; not used up

examTips: Always explain using collision theory — don't just say 'more collisions', explain WHY.
Catalyst lowers activation energy — it does NOT affect the overall energy change.
Temperature affects both frequency AND energy of collisions — mention both.
commonMistakes: Saying 'more collisions' without explaining why the factor causes this.
Thinking catalysts change the overall ΔH — they only lower activation energy.
Forgetting catalysts are not used up in the reaction.

Equilibrium.intro: Some reactions are reversible — they can proceed in both directions. At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal and concentrations remain constant.

sections.title: Reversible Reactions
points: Shown by ⇌ symbol
Both forward and reverse reactions occur simultaneously
At equilibrium: rate of forward = rate of reverse
Concentrations of reactants and products remain constant (but not necessarily equal)
Equilibrium is dynamic — reactions still happening in both directions

sections.title: Le Chatelier's Principle
sections.text: If conditions change, equilibrium shifts to oppose the change:
points: Increase temperature → shifts towards endothermic direction
Decrease temperature → shifts towards exothermic direction
Increase pressure → shifts towards side with fewer moles of gas
Increase concentration of a substance → shifts away from that substance
Catalyst → equilibrium reached faster but position UNCHANGED

keyTerms.def: A reaction that can proceed in both forward and reverse directions
State where forward and reverse rates are equal and concentrations are constant
If conditions change, equilibrium shifts to counteract the change

examTips: Catalyst speeds up reaching equilibrium but does NOT shift the position.
Changing pressure only affects equilibrium if there are different numbers of gas moles on each side.
'Dynamic' means reactions are still occurring — just at equal rates.
commonMistakes: Saying catalyst shifts equilibrium position — it does not.
Confusing dynamic equilibrium (still reacting) with no reaction occurring.
Saying concentrations are equal at equilibrium — they are constant, not necessarily equal.
